OSCAR APPEAL JUDGMENT

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Oscar PIstorius's Appeal Judgment is expected to be delivered in the first week of December. Will his sentenced be changed to murder?

Summary:
In the first week of November the world's media have gathered again - this time in Bloemfontein at the Supreme Court of Appeal to hear agruments from both the state and the defence. The State had been granted leave to appeal Oscar's verdict of culpable homicide and had argued in front of a full bench of appeal court Judges that Oscar's verdict should be changed to murder.

Further information:
The State argued that Judged Masipa misapplied the legal principle of dolus eventualis and that Oscar, by firing the four shots through the toilet door, should have foreseen that he would at least injure, or kill the person behind the door - irrespective whether it was Reeva or not.

The Defence argues that the State was trying to reintroduce of dolus directus.

All the Appeal Court Justices asked questions for clarification, but it was especially Justice Leach who time and again returned to the theme of dolus eventualis. And Barry Roux even went as far as to admit that maybe Oscar should have foreseen that he would injure, or probably, possibly kill someone behind the door when he fired four shots through the toilet door.

But Roux also argued that everything should be seen as a whole - how anxious Oscar was on the night of the shooting, his anxiety disorder and that he was truly fearful.

Head Justice Leach reserved judgment and the world's media and the Pistorius family is awaiting the judgment - will he go back to prison or not? And for how long? Because if the Appeal Court Justices overturn the verdict to murder, they would refer the matter back to Judge Masipa for sentencing. And that could take a long time. He would have to hand himself over or be re-arrested within 48 hours after the order of the court, he would have to re-apply for bail and then the matter needs to be placed back onto the court role of the North Gauteng High Court for Judge Masipa to sentence him. The defence is eligible to call witnesses in mitigation of sentence again and the state in aggravation of sentence. Retired Judge Fred Beckly recently said the process could take as long as two years.

And the legal minds in the country really hoped that clarity would be given in regard with the legal principle dolus eventualis.

OSCAR APPEAL JUDGMENT SCRIPT

PRODUCER: ESTE DE KLERK

JUSTICE ERIC LEACH: This case involves the human tragedy of Shakespearean proportions. The young man overcomes huge physical disabilities to reach Olympian heights as an athlete. He meets a young woman of great natural beauty and a successful model. All is destroyed when he takes her life. The court found the accused to have been a very poor witness. One does really not know what his explanation is having fired the fatal shots. I have no doubt that in firing the fatal shots the accused must have foreseen and therefore did foresee that whoever was behind the toilet door, might die, but reconciled himself to that event occurring and gambled with that person's life. He ought to have been convicted not of culpable homicide on that count but of murder.

JOHN LINK: It took Justice Leach 45 minutes to deliver the SCA’s ruling on the Oscar appeal. 45 minutes to explain how Judge Masipa had incorrectly applied Dolus Eventualis and why the athlete was guilty of murder. 45 minutes to end one chapter in the Oscar-story and to write the opening sentences of the next one.

The judgment by the five Appeal Court Justices was unanimous. And retired Judge Joos Hefer, who sat on the bench for 27 years, nineteen of those in the Appeal Court, says this carries a lot of weight.

JUDGE JOOS HEFER: In all important cases, you always try to get the agreement of all judges because even if one of them disagrees it shows there is some uncertainty in somebody's mind.

It’s been just more than a year since Oscar Pistorius sat sobbing in the North Gauteng High Court while Judge Thokozile Masipa acquitted him on the murder charge he stood trial for.
Instead, she found him guilty on the lesser charge of culpable homicide.
He was imprisoned for one day less than a year, and released in October to serve the remainder of his five-year sentence under correctional supervision and house arrest.

But now he would be stripped of his partial freedom again.
Not only is he now labeled a murderer, but he’s likely to return to the confined space of a prison cell soon.

JOHN PRISON LINK: So this is the cell where Oscar spent his close to one year behind bars. It’s fairly basic, a bed, it got a toilet in the corner, a steel basin and a small cupboard. As far as the dimensions are concerned, a little bit more than arm-width and slightly longer length ways. All in all, basic and pretty small.

Before Correctional Services escorted a large media contingent on tour in the Kgosi Mampuru II prison on Tuesday, Carte Blanche was granted access to visit the prison last week after we raised questions and wanted clarification on whether Oscar indeed received preferential treatment.

JOHN LINK PRISON: BATHROOM: During Oscar’s incarceration, reports emerged on an international broadcaster that he’d been offered special privileges, for example that he’d been given new gym equipment and that a bath had been built in his cell. Well, that is clearly not the case, because this is the bath in question, it’s a communal bath and can be used by any of the inmates in the hospital wing.

It was a trial that lasted eight months - the first ever to be televised.
Thirty-seven witnesses testified and Oscar was also sent for psychiatric evaluation.

In December last year, Judge Masipa granted chief prosecutor, Gerrie Nel and his team, leave to Appeal her verdict.
On November, the 3rd, arguments by the State and Defence were heard by a full bench of Justices at the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein.
And on Thursday this week, Justice Eric Leach - who had written the judgment - sealed Oscar’s fate: he murdered Reeva, having had criminal intent of dolus eventualis.

JOHN LINK:How does someone pick up a gun, fire four shot into a confined space and not foresee that someone else was going to be killed? A question that cuts to the very heart of Dolus Eventualis and one discussed across the country ever since Oscar Pistorius was found guilty on the lesser charge of culpable homicide. But Justice Leach said that Judge Masipa’s disregard of Dolus Eventualis was a misdirection.

JUSTICE ERIC LEACH: I find the reasoning in this passage to be confusing in various aspects. The rhetorical question how could the accused reasonably have foreseen that the shots he fired would kill the deceased or whoever was behind the door, wrongly applies an objective rather than a subjective approach to the question of dolus.

And that is a fairly strong indictment in the SCA’s judgment, says retired Judge Fred Beckley, who sat on the Free State High Court bench for 24 years.

JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: If you intend on killing A and accidentally kill B, you can't say: well, I'm not guilty of the murder of B because I never intended killing him, I intended to kill A". It doesn’t work that way.

Justice Leach said the issue was not whether Oscar had foreseen that Reeva might be in the cubicle when he fired, but “whether there was a person behind the door who might possibly be killed by his actions”.

JUSTICE LEACH: The trial court misdirected itself as to the appropriate legal issue. An incorrect test was applied.

JOHN: Judge, Were you surprised by the confusion that came out of Judge Masipa's ruling on that particular issue?

JUDGE HEFER: To me it wasn’t confusion. In my view, I think she made a mess of it. Dealing with it right from the outset with the foreseeability of whom, that is where she made her first mistake and that dented her whole approach to the question. So, me it was a mystery how she eventually came to her conclusion.

(14”) Oscar had always maintained that he believed there was an intruder in the house, but Justice Leach said “the identity of his victim is irrelevant to his guilt”. He said Oscar never offered acceptable explanation for firing the shots.

JUSTICE LEACH: And he never offered an acceptable explanation for having done so. As a matter of common sense at the time the fatal shots were fired, the possibility of the death of the person behind the door was clearly an obvious result and in firing not one but four shots, such a result became even more likely. But that is exactly what the accused did.

JOHN LINK: The second issue the SCA had to grapple with was whether Judge Masipa had ignored key circumstantial evidence in arriving at her verdict. And while some might consider that a question of fact rather than law, the Supreme Court found that the one informs the other and that evidence cannot simply be ignored.

[APPEAL COURT HEARING: 3 NOVEMBER 2015/GERRIE NEL]: The court ignored the evidence, the most important circumstantial evidence that will make the accused’s version not reasonably, possibly true - impossible.

JUSTICE LEACH: There seems to me to be no difference in principle between the exclusion of relevant evidence by ruling it inadmissible. And excluding such evidence once admitted, by not taking it into account to decide the issues in dispute, in either event the judicial process becomes flawed by regard not being had to material, which might affect the outcome.

More than a year since Judge Masipa’s judgment, the importance of the evidence of the State’s star witness, police forensic expert Captain Chris Mangena, was finally recognised.

JUSTICE LEACH: All the shots fired through the door would almost inevitably have struck a person behind it. There had effectively been nowhere for the deceased to hide.

JUDGE JOOS HEFER: How can you arrive at any decision whether you're looking for a conviction on culpable homicide or on murder, you cannot ignore important facts

JUSTICE LEACH: All of this was circumstantial evidence crucial to a decision on whether the accused at the time he fired the fatal four shots must have foreseen and therefore did foresee the potentially fatal consequences of his actions.

And yet, Justice Leach said, Judge Masipa and her assessors seemingly ignored this evidence in their assessment of the presence of dolus eventualis.

JUSTICE LEACH: Had it been taken into account, the decision in regard to the absence of dolus eventualis may very well have been different.

The failure to take it into account, must be regarded as an error of law, Justice Leach said.

JOHN LINK: The prosecution also asked the SCA to rule on whether Judge Masipa had relied on one of Oscar’s versions to arrive at her verdict. But by the time Justice Leach arrived at that issue, Oscar’s fate had already been sealed.

In arguing Oscar’s case at the Appeal Court, Barry Roux, emphasized that Oscar, extremely anxious and in a vulnerable state on his stumps, fired because of a perceived danger. But Justice Leach ruled that in his view, this couldn’t be accepted.

JUDGE BECKLEY: Whether it was in self-defence, whether it was because the fact that he was scared that there was an assailant or that he suffered from a loss of memory as to why he fired, we will never know.

Justice Leach said the interest of justice required that a person should be convicted of the actual crime he had committed and not of lesser offences.
As a last word on the matter, the Appeal Court said that its findings “shouldn’t be seen as an adverse comment” upon which Judge Masipa’s competence and ability.

JUSTICE LEACH: The fact that the appeal has succeeded is not to be regarded as a slight upon the trial judge who is to be congratulated for the manner in which she conducted the proceedings.

Now guilty of murder, Oscar’s sentence for culpable homicide was also set aside.
On Friday, the National Prosecuting Authority said he’d have to appear in court for a new bail application as a matter of urgency.

JOHN LINK: The case now returns to the High Court for sentencing proceedings, although it is unlikely when that will take place. It will be up to Judge Masipa how much more time Oscar will spend behind bars.

JUDGE BECKLEY: Fifteen years is the minimum sentence for a crime such as the one that Pistorius is being convicted of. If she does find that there are these compelling and substantial circumstances, she could impose a lesser sentence, possibly consider a sentence of between twelve and fourteen years.

JOHN LINK: GUILTY: Now that the Appeals Court has changed the verdict to murder, it’s likely that Oscar will return to Kgosi Mampuru. In fact, he’ll probably return to this wing and be housed in one of these two cells.

And Barry and June Steenkamp say that even though nothing can bring Reeva back, justice had finally been done.

______________


OUTRO:
It’s believed that Oscar’s bail application will take place early next week and that his arrest wouldn’t be enforced until then.
